questions.text_english:
(1) On the first clear September day, towards the end of the rains, I visited the pine knoll, my place of peace and power.

(2) It was months since I'd last been there. Trips to the plains, a crisis in my affairs, involvements with other people and their troubles, and an entire monsoon had come between me and the grassy, pine-topped slope facing the Hill of Fairies (Pari Tibba to the locals). Now I tramped through late monsoon foliage — tall ferns, bushes festooned with flowering convolvulus — and crossed the stream by way of its little bridge of stones before climbing the steep hill to the pine slope.

(3) When the trees saw me, they made as if to turn in my direction. A puff of wind came across the valley from the distant snows. A long-tailed blue magpie took alarm and flew noisily out of an oak tree. The cicadas were suddenly silent. But the trees remembered me. They bowed gently in the breeze and beckoned me nearer, welcoming me home. Three pines, a straggling oak and a wild cherry. I went among them and acknowledged their welcome with a touch of my hand against their trunks — the cherry's smooth and polished; the pine's patterned and whorled; the oak's rough, gnarled, full of experience. He'd been there the longest, and the wind had bent his upper branches and twisted a few, so that he looked shaggy and undistinguished. But like the philosopher who is careless about his dress and appearance, the oak has secrets, a hidden wisdom. He has learnt the art of survival!

(4) While the oak and the pines are older than me and have been here many years, the cherry tree is exactly seven years old. I know, because I planted it.

(5) One day I had this cherry seed in my hand, and on an impulse I thrust it into the soft earth, and then went away and forgot all about it. A few months later I found a tiny cherry tree in the long grass. I did not expect it to survive. But the following year it was two feet tall. And then some goats ate its leaves, and a grass cutter's scythe injured the stem, and I was sure it would wither away. But it renewed itself, sprang up even faster; and within three years it was a healthy, growing tree, about five feet tall.

(6) I left the hills for two years — forced by circumstances to make a living in the city — but this time I did not forget the cherry tree. I thought about it fairly often, sent telepathic messages of encouragement in its direction. And when, a couple of years ago, I returned in the autumn, my heart did a somersault when I found my tree sprinkled with pale pink blossom. (The Himalayan cherry flowers in November.) And later, when the fruit was ripe, the tree was visited by finches, tits, bulbuls and other small birds, all come to feast on the sour, red cherries.

(7) Last summer I spent a night on the pine knoll, sleeping on the grass beneath the cherry tree. I lay awake for hours, listening to the chatter of the stream and the occasional tonk-tonk of nightjars, and watching through the branches overhead, the stars turning in the sky. And I felt the power of the sky and the earth, and the power of a small cherry seed...

(8) And so when the rains are over, this is where I come, that I might feel the peace and power of this place.

(9) This is where I will write my stories. I can see everything from here — my cottage across the valley; behind and above me, the town and the bazaar, straddling the ridge; to the left, the high mountains and the twisting road to the source of the great river; below me, the little stream and the path to the village; ahead, the Hill of Fairies and the fields beyond; the wide valley below, and another range of hills and then the distant plains. I can even see Prem Singh in the garden, putting the mattresses out in the sun.

(10) From here he is just a speck on the far hill, but I know it is Prem by the way he stands. A man may have a hundred disguises, but in the end it is his posture that gives him away. Like my grandfather, who was a master of disguise and successfully roamed the bazaars as fruit vendor or basket maker. But we could always recognize him because of his pronounced slouch.

(11) Prem Singh doesn't slouch, but he has this habit of looking up at the sky (regardless of whether it's cloudy or clear), and at the moment he's looking at the sky.

(12) Eight years with Prem. He was just a sixteen-year-old boy when I first saw him, and now he has a wife and child.

(13) I had been in the cottage for just over a year... He stood on the landing outside the kitchen door. A tall boy, dark, with good teeth and brown, deep-set eyes, dressed smartly in white drill — his only change of clothes. Looking for a job. I liked the look of him, but — 'I already have someone working for me,' I said. 'Yes, sir. He is my uncle.' In the hills, everyone is a brother or an uncle. 'You don't want me to dismiss your uncle?' 'No, sir. But he says you can find a job for me.' 'I'll try. I'll make inquiries. Have you just come from your village?' 'Yes. Yesterday I walked ten miles to Pauri. There I got a bus.' 'Sit down. Your uncle will make some tea.' He sat down on the steps, removed his white keds, wriggled his toes. His feet were both long and broad, large feet but not ugly. He was unusually clean for a hill boy. And taller than most.

(14) 'Your name is ...?' 'Prem Singh.' 'All right, Prem, I will try to do something for you.' I did not see him for a couple of weeks. I forgot about finding him a job. But when I met him again, on the road to the bazaar, he told me that he had got a temporary job in the Survey, looking after the surveyor's tents. 'Next week we will be going to Rajasthan,' he said. 'It will be very hot. Have you been in the desert before?' 'No, sir.' 'It is not like the hills. And it is far from home.' 'I know. But I have no choice in the matter.'
questions.instruction_line: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any twelve out of the fifteen questions given below.
questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any twelve out of the fifteen questions given below.
questions.solution: Passage-based question set. Answers are provided in sub_questions.
questions.topic: Prose Passage — Nature and Human Connection

sub_questions.text_english: Which of the following is not true about the author?

options_english.A: He visited the pine knoll every year at the end of the rains.
options_english.B: His visit was delayed because of his engagement with other people's problems.
options_english.C: He had not visited the pine knoll for months.
options_english.D: He visited the pine knoll on the first clear day of September.

sub_questions.solution: Option A is incorrect because the passage does not state that the author visited every year — in fact paragraph 2 says it had been months since his last visit, and he had been away for long periods due to trips, personal crises, and a monsoon. Options B, C, and D are all directly supported by paragraphs 2 and 1 respectively, making them true statements.

sub_questions.text_english: Choose a word from the passage which is an apt synonym for 'leaves of a plant or tree'. (Paragraph 2 and 3)
sub_questions.solution: The word 'foliage' means the leaves of a plant or tree, used in paragraph 2 where the author describes walking through 'late monsoon foliage'. Convolvulus is a flowering plant, cicadas are insects, and breeze refers to wind — none of these is a synonym for leaves.

sub_questions.text_english: The sentence 'I went among them and acknowledged their welcome with a touch of my hand against their trunks,' reflects that the author was _______ to be back. (Paragraph 3)
sub_questions.solution: Option A is correct. The gesture of touching the trunks affectionately and acknowledging their welcome shows the author's happiness and nostalgia at returning to a beloved place. The trees are personified as welcoming him home, and his response is warm and emotionally engaged — the opposite of confusion, conflict, or indifference.

sub_questions.text_english: The arrival of the author at the pine knoll disturbed the _________.
sub_questions.solution: Option D is correct. Paragraph 3 clearly states that a long-tailed blue magpie took alarm and flew noisily out of the oak tree, and the cicadas were suddenly silent — both creatures were disturbed by the author's arrival. The other options are not described as being disturbed.

sub_questions.text_english: Statement 1: The oak looked shaggy and undistinguished. Statement 2: The wind had bent his upper branches and twisted a few.

options_english.A: Both Statements 1 and 2 are correct and Statement 2 is the reason for Statement 1.
options_english.B: Both Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but Statement 2 is not the reason for Statement 1.
options_english.C: Statement 1 is correct, but Statement 2 is incorrect.

sub_questions.solution: Option A is correct. Both statements are factually accurate as described in paragraph 3. Moreover, the passage directly links the wind bending and twisting the oak's branches as the cause of it looking shaggy and undistinguished — making Statement 2 the explicit reason for Statement 1.

sub_questions.text_english: The phrase 'on an impulse' tells you that the author planted the cherry tree _________.

options_english.B: on instructions by the orchard owner

sub_questions.solution: Option C is correct. The phrase 'on an impulse' means acting spontaneously without forethought or planning. Paragraph 5 confirms this — the author thrust the seed into the earth impulsively and then 'went away and forgot all about it', which is the opposite of careful research, instructions, or pre-conditions.

sub_questions.text_english: The author was convinced that the cherry tree would wither away because ________.

options_english.A: there was no monsoon that year
options_english.B: the cicadas had eaten its leaves
options_english.C: the grass cutter had damaged the stem
options_english.D: the branch of the oak tree fell on it

sub_questions.solution: Option C is correct. Paragraph 5 states that goats ate the tree's leaves and a grass cutter's scythe injured the stem, after which the author was sure it would wither away. Options A, B, and D are not mentioned in the passage as reasons for the author's concern.

sub_questions.text_english: What literary device is used in the phrase 'my heart did a somersault'?
sub_questions.solution: Option B is correct. The phrase 'my heart did a somersault' is an example of personification, as the heart — a non-living organ — is given the human ability to perform a somersault, expressing the author's sudden overwhelming joy. It is not a simile (no comparison using 'like' or 'as'), not irony, and not alliteration.

sub_questions.text_english: The author believes that spending time on the pine knoll gives him ________.
sub_questions.solution: Option D is correct. The very first paragraph describes the pine knoll as the author's 'place of peace and power', and paragraph 9 states this is where he will write his stories — indicating inspiration. Paragraphs 7 and 8 reinforce that the knoll provides a sense of calm and creative energy, not anxiety, melancholy, or mere companionship.

sub_questions.text_english: Describe the sight that the author sees from the pine knoll.

key_points: His cottage across the valley
The town and bazaar on the ridge behind him
High mountains and the twisting road to the great river's source
The stream and the path to the village below
The Hill of Fairies, fields, wide valley, distant plains, and Prem Singh in the garden

sub_questions.solution: From the pine knoll, the author commands a sweeping panoramic view. He can see his cottage across the valley, and behind him the town and bazaar straddling the ridge. To his left lie the high mountains and the winding road to the source of the great river, while below him flows the little stream and the path leading to the village. Ahead stretches the Hill of Fairies, the fields beyond it, the wide valley, another range of hills, and finally the distant plains. He can even spot Prem Singh in the garden placing mattresses in the sun.

sub_questions.text_english: The author emphasizes on the vivid and sensorial images of nature in his writings. Justify with two examples from the extract.

key_points: Tactile imagery — textures of tree trunks (cherry smooth, pine patterned, oak rough and gnarled)
Auditory imagery — the chatter of the stream and the tonk-tonk of nightjars heard while lying under the cherry tree

sub_questions.solution: The author uses rich sensorial imagery throughout the passage. In paragraph 3, he describes the textures of the tree trunks — the cherry's smooth and polished bark, the pine's patterned and whorled surface, and the oak's rough, gnarled trunk — engaging the reader's sense of touch. In paragraph 7, he creates vivid auditory imagery by describing the chatter of the stream and the occasional tonk-tonk of nightjars heard while lying under the cherry tree, immersing the reader in the sounds of the night.

sub_questions.text_english: What was the intention of Prem Singh when he met the author for the first time?

key_points: Prem Singh came to ask the author to find him a job
He had come from his village and his uncle, who worked for the author, had suggested approaching him

sub_questions.solution: When Prem Singh met the author for the first time, his intention was to seek employment. He had walked ten miles from his village to Pauri and then taken a bus, arriving at the author's cottage looking for a job. His uncle, who was already working for the author, had encouraged him to approach the author, suggesting that he might be able to find something for him.

sub_questions.text_english: What is the posture or mannerism of Prem Singh that the author refers to?

key_points: Prem Singh has the habit of looking up at the sky regardless of the weather
This distinctive mannerism allows the author to identify him even from a distance

sub_questions.solution: The author notes that Prem Singh has a distinctive habit of looking up at the sky, whether it is cloudy or clear. This characteristic mannerism is so recognizable that even from a great distance — where Prem appears as just a speck on the far hill — the author can identify him by this gesture. It contrasts with the author's grandfather, who was identifiable by his pronounced slouch.

sub_questions.text_english: State whether the following opinion is True or False. The author did not give Prem Singh a job initially because of his slouching posture.
sub_questions.solution: This statement is False. The author did not give Prem Singh a job initially simply because he already had someone working for him — Prem's uncle. Paragraph 13 clearly shows the author said 'I already have someone working for me.' Furthermore, paragraph 11 explicitly states that Prem Singh does not slouch, ruling out any connection between a slouching posture and the refusal of employment.

sub_questions.text_english: Why does Prem Singh tell the author, 'I have no choice in the matter'?

key_points: Prem has taken a temporary job with the Survey department that requires him to go to Rajasthan
He has no permanent employment and must take what is available, even if it means going far from his hill home

sub_questions.solution: Prem Singh says 'I have no choice in the matter' because he has secured only a temporary job with the Survey department, and the work requires him to travel to Rajasthan — a place far from his home in the hills and a vastly different environment. As someone without steady employment, he cannot afford to turn down available work even though the journey is long, the climate harsh, and the desert landscape unfamiliar to a hill person like him.

questions.text_english:
The Rain

We left that old ungainly house
When my dog died there, after
The burial, after the rose
Flowered twice, pulling it by its
Roots and carting it with our books,
Clothes and chairs in a hurry.
We live in a new house now,
And, the roofs do not leak, but, when
It rains here, I see the rain drench
That empty house, I hear it fall
Where my puppy now lies.
Alone..
questions.instruction_line: Based on your understanding of the poem, answer any four out of the five questions given below.
questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the poem, answer any four out of the five questions given below.
questions.solution: Poem-based question set. Answers are provided in sub_questions.
questions.topic: The Rain by Kamala Das — Memory and Loss

sub_questions.text_english: The image of the old ungainly house evokes the feeling of:
sub_questions.solution: Option D is correct. The old house is associated with the death of the poet's dog, burial, and an abrupt departure — all deeply sorrowful events. The word 'ungainly' itself suggests something awkward and unappealing, and the memories tied to it are painful rather than optimistic, comforting, or relieving.

sub_questions.text_english: The line 'but, when it rains here, I see the rain drench that empty house' indicates that memories are ________.
sub_questions.solution: Option C is correct. Even after moving to a new house, the poet still vividly visualises and hears the rain falling on the old empty house. The fact that these images persist despite physical relocation shows that the memories are enduring — lasting and not easily forgotten — rather than fading, transient, or fleeting.

sub_questions.text_english: How does the poet contrast the new house with the earlier one?
sub_questions.solution: Option A is correct. The poet contrasts the two houses by noting that 'the roofs do not leak' in the new house, implying the old house was structurally unsound and dilapidated. The new house is thus sturdy, while the old one was leaky and deteriorating. No textual evidence supports contrasts of size, cost, or modernity versus tradition.

sub_questions.text_english: Complete the sentence appropriately. The poem ends with the poignant final word 'Alone' to emphasize ___________.

fill_values: the isolation and abandonment of the dead puppy in the empty house, intensifying the poet's grief and guilt

sub_questions.solution: The poem ends with the poignant final word 'Alone' to emphasize the isolation and abandonment of the dead puppy left behind in the empty house. The family moved away with all their possessions — books, clothes, chairs, even the rose — but the puppy remains there, buried, solitary, in a house no one inhabits. The word resonates with the poet's lingering guilt and unresolved grief over leaving the animal behind.

sub_questions.text_english: Explain how, in the above poem, the image of rain serves as a catalyst of memory.

key_points: Rain in the new house triggers a mental vision of the old house being drenched
The sound and sight of rain transport the poet emotionally back to the place of loss
Rain becomes the bridge between the present and the painful past

sub_questions.solution: In Kamala Das's poem, rain acts as a powerful catalyst of memory. When it rains in the new house, the poet is transported back to the old one — she sees the rain drench that empty house and hears it fall where her puppy now lies buried. The rain in the present moment triggers an involuntary, vivid recollection of grief and loss, making the past feel immediate and inescapable. Rain thus becomes the sensory bridge between the poet's current life and her irretrievable sorrow.

questions.text_english:
Modern technology plays a vital role in reducing road accidents and improving traffic flow. A study in three major cities — Delhi, Bengaluru, and Mumbai — found that using smart cameras, GPS tracking, and automated traffic lights improved safety significantly. AI-based monitoring systems detect traffic violations and alert authorities instantly. Drivers using navigation apps report fewer delays and accidents. Advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), like lane departure warnings and automatic braking, have made vehicles safer.

Table: City | Accidents Before Tech Use (per month) | Accidents After Tech Use (per month) | Reduction %
Delhi | 320 | 220 | 31
Bengaluru | 280 | 190 | 32
Mumbai | 350 | 240 | 31

Mobile apps now alert drivers about congested routes and road hazards. In India, the introduction of e-challan systems has improved traffic rule enforcement and reduced human error. Moreover, data from surveillance cameras helps authorities identify accident-prone areas for quick intervention. Technology not only saves time but also saves lives by ensuring safer, smarter roads.

questions.instruction_line_english: Based on your understanding of the passage, answer any four out of the five questions given below.
questions.solution: Factual passage-based question set. Answers are provided in sub_questions.
questions.image_description: A three-column data table comparing road accidents before and after technology use in three Indian cities: Delhi (320 to 220, 31% reduction), Bengaluru (280 to 190, 32% reduction), and Mumbai (350 to 240, 31% reduction).

sub_questions.text_english: Fill in the blank by selecting the appropriate option. It is important to use technology in road management as it is ________ for decreasing road accidents.
sub_questions.solution: Option A is correct. The very first sentence of the passage states that 'Modern technology plays a vital role in reducing road accidents', making 'vital' the most appropriate word. Options C and D are antonyms of the intended meaning, and 'obligatory' implies a legal duty rather than functional importance.

sub_questions.text_english: How does AI help traffic management?

key_points: AI-based monitoring systems detect traffic violations in real time
They alert authorities instantly, enabling quick action

sub_questions.solution: AI helps traffic management by enabling real-time monitoring of roads. AI-based systems can detect traffic violations as they happen and instantly send alerts to the relevant authorities, allowing for prompt enforcement and intervention. This reduces human error in traffic monitoring and makes law enforcement more efficient and responsive.

sub_questions.text_english: State True or False: According to the data given in the table, accidents in Bengaluru were the lowest among the given cities at 190 and the reduction percentage was also the least.
sub_questions.solution: This statement is False. While it is true that accidents in Bengaluru after technology use were 190 — the lowest among the three cities — the reduction percentage in Bengaluru was 32%, which is actually the highest, not the least. Delhi and Mumbai both had a 31% reduction. Therefore the second part of the statement is incorrect.

sub_questions.text_english: Complete the sentence appropriately. Technology has helped improve road safety through _________.

fill_values: smart cameras, GPS tracking, automated traffic lights, AI monitoring, navigation apps, ADAS features, e-challan systems, and surveillance data that identifies accident-prone areas

sub_questions.solution: Technology has helped improve road safety through a range of tools and systems including smart cameras, GPS tracking, automated traffic lights, AI-based violation monitoring, navigation apps, Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) such as lane departure warnings and automatic braking, e-challan enforcement, and surveillance data that helps authorities identify and address accident-prone areas.

sub_questions.text_english: State a point in support for the given opinion. The role of technology in enhancing road safety and traffic management cannot be undermined.

key_points: Data from three cities shows significant reductions of 31-32% in monthly accidents after technology was introduced
Multiple technologies work together creating a comprehensive safety ecosystem

sub_questions.solution: The data presented in the passage strongly supports this opinion. In all three cities — Delhi, Bengaluru, and Mumbai — the introduction of technology led to a significant reduction in monthly accidents ranging from 31% to 32%. This measurable, consistent improvement across different urban environments demonstrates that technology is not just supplementary but central to making roads safer, and its role in traffic management clearly cannot be underestimated.

questions.text_english: Transform the following sentences according to the instructions given against each one. Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.
questions.instruction_line: Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.
questions.instruction_line_english: Attempt any eight out of the ten questions that follow.
questions.solution: Sentence transformation grammar exercise. Answers are provided in sub_questions.

sub_questions.text_english: The police arrived at the spot. The protesters ran helter-skelter. (Start with: Hardly ………..)

fill_values: Hardly had the police arrived at the spot when the protesters ran helter-skelter.

sub_questions.solution: The rule applied here is inversion after a negative adverb. When 'Hardly' begins a sentence, the auxiliary verb is inverted before the subject (Hardly + had + subject + past participle), and the second clause uses 'when'. Full sentence: Hardly had the police arrived at the spot when the protesters ran helter-skelter.

sub_questions.text_english: Slum dwellers are the worst-hit people in the floods. (Start with: The worst-hit ………..)

fill_values: The worst-hit people in the floods are slum dwellers.

sub_questions.solution: This transformation involves fronting the complement to the beginning of the sentence. The subject and predicate are simply inverted to place the focus on 'the worst-hit people'. Full sentence: The worst-hit people in the floods are slum dwellers.

sub_questions.text_english: She started reading. She fell asleep. (Start with: No sooner ………..)

fill_values: No sooner had she started reading than she fell asleep.

sub_questions.solution: The rule applied is inversion after 'No sooner', a negative adverbial. The structure is: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + subject + simple past. Full sentence: No sooner had she started reading than she fell asleep.

sub_questions.text_english: He won't join the team unless he gets a uniform. (Start with: If ………..)

fill_values: If he does not get a uniform, he won't join the team.

sub_questions.solution: 'Unless' means 'if not', so the transformation replaces 'unless' with 'if...not' while preserving the original meaning. Full sentence: If he does not get a uniform, he won't join the team.

sub_questions.text_english: If you do not study hard, you will fail. (Rewrite using: Unless ………..)

fill_values: Unless you study hard, you will fail.

sub_questions.solution: 'Unless' is equivalent to 'if not', so 'If you do not' is replaced with 'Unless you'. The negative is removed from the conditional clause. Full sentence: Unless you study hard, you will fail.

sub_questions.text_english: He is very proud. He will not ask for help. (Rewrite using: 'too')

fill_values: He is too proud to ask for help.

sub_questions.solution: The 'too...to' structure expresses that an extreme quality prevents an action. The two sentences are combined as: adjective preceded by 'too' + infinitive. Full sentence: He is too proud to ask for help.

sub_questions.text_english: I have never seen such a beautiful painting before. (Start with: Never ………..)

fill_values: Never before have I seen such a beautiful painting.

sub_questions.solution: When 'Never' begins a sentence, subject-auxiliary inversion is required. The auxiliary 'have' moves before the subject 'I'. Full sentence: Never before have I seen such a beautiful painting.

sub_questions.text_english: Have you seen my car keys, he asked. (Start with: He asked ………..)

fill_values: He asked if I had seen his car keys.

sub_questions.solution: Reported speech for a yes/no question requires 'if' or 'whether', backshift of tense (have to had), and change of pronouns (you to I, my to his). Full sentence: He asked if I had seen his car keys.

sub_questions.text_english: She wants to become a musician. She wants to become a skilled writer. (Combine using: as well as)

fill_values: She wants to become a musician as well as a skilled writer.

sub_questions.solution: 'As well as' is used to add one element to another without implying a hierarchy. The repeated subject and verb are removed and the two objects are joined. Full sentence: She wants to become a musician as well as a skilled writer.

sub_questions.text_english: The Principal said, "Saturday will be a working day." (Start with: The Principal informed ………..)

fill_values: The Principal informed us that Saturday would be a working day.

sub_questions.solution: Reported speech with 'informed' requires an indirect object ('us'), the conjunction 'that', and tense backshift (will to would). Full sentence: The Principal informed us that Saturday would be a working day.

sub_questions.text_english: 'Digital divide' creates inequalities in access to information, resources and opportunities, impacting education, employment and social participation. Write an analytical essay in 120 - 150 words on the impact of 'digital divide' in India and suggest ways to bridge it. Provide examples to illustrate your point of view.

key_points: Define digital divide and its relevance in India
Impact on education — rural students lack devices and internet
Impact on employment — digital illiteracy limits job opportunities
Impact on social participation — exclusion from digital governance
Suggest solutions — affordable internet, digital literacy programs, government initiatives

sub_questions.solution:
The Digital Divide in India

The digital divide refers to the gap between those who have access to modern technology and the internet and those who do not. In India, this divide is stark: urban households enjoy high-speed connectivity while millions in rural areas remain offline. During the COVID-19 pandemic, students in remote regions could not attend online classes due to lack of devices and internet access, widening educational inequalities.

In terms of employment, digital illiteracy limits opportunities for millions, as most modern jobs require basic technological competence. Moreover, government schemes like Direct Benefit Transfers and digital IDs are inaccessible to those without smartphones or internet.

To bridge this gap, India must expand affordable broadband through initiatives like BharatNet, promote digital literacy in schools, and subsidise devices for marginalised communities. Bridging the digital divide is essential to ensure inclusive growth and equal opportunity for all citizens.

sub_questions.text_english: Deforestation, urbanization, habitat loss, increased human population density and competition for resources have led to human – animal conflict. Discuss the importance of planned urbanization with reference to wildlife protection and environmental conservation in an essay of 120 - 150 words. Suggest how habitat loss can be contained and coexistence be maintained.

key_points: Define human-animal conflict and its causes
Importance of planned urbanization in reducing habitat intrusion
Role of wildlife corridors and buffer zones
Suggest community involvement and eco-sensitive zoning
Conclusion emphasizing coexistence

sub_questions.solution:
Planned Urbanization and Wildlife Conservation

The rapid expansion of cities and agricultural land has pushed wildlife to the brink. Elephants raid crops, leopards enter towns, and tigers lose territory — all consequences of unchecked deforestation and habitat destruction. Human-animal conflict is no longer an exception; it is a growing crisis.

Planned urbanization is the solution. By designating eco-sensitive zones and establishing wildlife corridors that connect forest patches, we can allow animals to move freely without encroaching on human settlements. Buffer zones between protected areas and residential localities can reduce direct encounters.

Habitat loss can be contained by enforcing strict land-use policies, reforesting degraded areas, and involving local communities as conservation stakeholders. Coexistence requires awareness, compensation mechanisms for affected farmers, and humane conflict-resolution protocols. Sustainable development and wildlife protection must advance together for the survival of both people and animals.

sub_questions.text_english: 'Bagless days' is an educational initiative suggested in various workshops where students attend school without carrying their usual school bags and textbooks. Its aim is to reduce physical strain, enhance mental well-being, reduce academic pressure, encourage experiential learning and skill development. Write an essay in 120 - 150 words on the advantages and challenges of this new initiative.

key_points: Introduce the bagless days initiative
Advantages — reduced physical strain, less stress, promotes experiential learning
Advantages — fosters creativity and practical skills
Challenges — curriculum coverage, parental resistance, implementation in exam-focused system
Balanced conclusion

sub_questions.solution:
Bagless Days: Advantages and Challenges

The 'Bagless Days' initiative, which allows students to attend school without textbooks and bags, is a welcome step towards holistic education. Heavy schoolbags cause physical strain, including back problems among young children. By eliminating this burden occasionally, the initiative directly improves students' physical comfort.

Beyond the physical, bagless days reduce academic pressure and provide space for experiential learning — field visits, art activities, group projects — that nurture creativity and practical skills often neglected in rote-based education.

However, the initiative also faces challenges. In an examination-driven system, parents and teachers may worry about curriculum gaps. Schools lacking resources for activity-based learning may struggle to plan meaningful bagless sessions. Resistance from stakeholders focused solely on academic performance can hinder implementation.

Despite these challenges, when properly planned, bagless days can transform the school experience, making learning joyful, engaging, and more meaningful for students.

sub_questions.text_english: Family and friends are crucial for our well-being, offering emotional support and a sense of belonging. They are vital for navigating life's challenges and maintaining a positive outlook. Write an article on the role of family and friends in your life in 120 - 150 words. You are Anoop/Anvita.

key_points: Introduce with a personal statement on importance of family and friends
Role of family — unconditional support, values, sense of belonging
Role of friends — companionship, shared experiences, encouragement
How they help navigate challenges and maintain positivity
Concluding reflection

sub_questions.solution:
The Pillars of My Life
By Anvita

In the journey of life, family and friends are the anchors that keep us grounded. My family has been my first and most enduring source of strength. From the warmth of home to the wisdom shared at the dinner table, they have shaped my values, given me identity, and stood by me in every difficulty without judgement or condition.

Friends, on the other hand, bring colour and laughter. They celebrate my successes and sit with me in my failures. When academic pressure feels overwhelming or uncertainty creeps in, a conversation with a trusted friend can restore perspective and hope.

Together, family and friends form a support system that no achievement can replace. They remind me that I am never alone in this world. Their love and companionship are not luxuries — they are necessities that define the quality of a life truly lived.

sub_questions.text_english: Taking cues from Kerala and Tamil Nadu Education Board initiative, your school conducted a seminar on 'water bell' system, providing short breaks (3 - 4 times a day), allowing students to hydrate and reduce the risk of heat-induced ailments. Write a report in 120 - 150 words on the event. You are Kanavi/Kanna, a reporter of The Times of India.

key_points: Headline and byline
Introduction — when, where, and what event
Details of the seminar — speakers, purpose of water bell
Benefits highlighted — hydration, reduced heat ailments
Conclusion — school's commitment to student well-being

sub_questions.solution:
School Hosts Seminar on 'Water Bell' System
By Kanna | The Times of India

New Delhi, June 10: In a commendable initiative inspired by the successful models of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, Delhi Public School hosted a seminar on the 'Water Bell' system on Friday. The event was attended by teachers, school health officials, and senior students.

The seminar highlighted the importance of mandatory hydration breaks — three to four times a day — during school hours, particularly in the sweltering summer months. Experts present at the event explained that inadequate water intake among students leads to fatigue, heatstroke, and poor concentration, adversely affecting academic performance.

The school principal announced that the water bell system would be formally introduced from the next academic session. 'Healthy students learn better,' she remarked. The initiative was warmly received by parents and students alike, who appreciated the school's commitment to holistic well-being over mere academic productivity.

sub_questions.text_english: Youth today can serve the nation through civic engagement, community service, volunteering, and cultivating skills to solve social problems. Write an article in 120 - 150 words on how youth can play a crucial role in empowering the nation through service.

key_points: Introduce youth as a powerful force for national change
Civic engagement — voting, awareness campaigns, policy advocacy
Community service — volunteering in education, health, environment
Skill cultivation — using professional skills to solve social problems
Call to action and inspiring conclusion

sub_questions.solution:
Youth: The Engine of National Empowerment

India is a young nation — over 65% of its population is below the age of 35. This demographic dividend is not merely a statistic; it is a transformative force waiting to be channelled. Today's youth have the energy, skills, and idealism to reshape the country, provided they choose service over indifference.

Civic engagement begins with awareness — understanding local issues, participating in community meetings, and exercising the right to vote. Beyond this, volunteering in education initiatives like teaching underprivileged children, participating in cleanliness drives, or working with NGOs addressing hunger and health can create tangible, grassroots change.

Digital skills, design thinking, and entrepreneurship can be deployed to solve social challenges at scale. When youth treat service not as an obligation but as an opportunity, they do not just empower communities — they build the very foundation of a stronger, more equitable nation.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': What prompted her to tell him to leave right away?

key_points: She had dreamed about him the previous night
Her dream gave her a strong conviction that he was in danger and must leave Vienna immediately

sub_questions.solution: In the story 'I Sell My Dreams', the woman was prompted to urge him to leave because she had dreamed about him the previous night. Her dream carried such a powerful sense of foreboding and danger that she felt an urgent conviction he must leave Vienna at once and not return for five years. Her belief in the prophetic nature of her dreams was absolute, and she acted on it immediately.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': Where did the author go, after leaving Vienna?

key_points: The author boarded the last train to Rome that same night.

sub_questions.solution: After leaving Vienna, the author boarded the last train to Rome that same night, acting immediately on the woman's warning without question or delay.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': Why does the author say he considered himself a survivor of some catastrophe he never experienced?

key_points: The woman's conviction was so powerful that it influenced his thinking entirely
He believed a disaster would have befallen him had he stayed in Vienna, even though it never actually occurred

sub_questions.solution: The author says he considered himself a survivor of a catastrophe he never experienced because the woman's conviction was so intense and persuasive that it reshaped his sense of reality. He came to believe that had he remained in Vienna, something terrible would have happened to him. Even though no actual catastrophe took place, the psychological impact of her warning made him feel as though he had narrowly escaped disaster.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': What do you infer about her attitude towards the author?

key_points: She genuinely cares about the author's safety and well-being
She takes her prophetic dreams seriously and feels responsible for warning those she dreams about

sub_questions.solution: Her attitude towards the author is one of genuine concern and protective care. She goes out of her way to warn him based solely on her dream, demonstrating that she takes her premonitions seriously and feels responsible for the safety of those she dreams about. Her conviction is so sincere that it compels the author to act immediately, suggesting a relationship of trust and deep emotional influence.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': Why did the author not return to Vienna?

key_points: He was deeply influenced by the woman's warning and internalized the belief that Vienna was unsafe
Having come to see himself as a survivor, he never felt the need or courage to return

sub_questions.solution: The author did not return to Vienna because the woman's warning had such a lasting psychological impact on him that it permanently altered his relationship with the city. He had so thoroughly absorbed her conviction that something catastrophic would befall him there that returning felt impossibly risky. Having mentally reframed himself as a survivor of an unseen disaster, Vienna remained a place of imagined danger for the rest of his life.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (a) — 'I Sell My Dreams': Which word is an apt synonym for 'conviction'?
sub_questions.solution: Option D, 'certainty', is the apt synonym for 'conviction'. In the extract, the woman's conviction refers to her firm, unwavering belief and certainty about the warning she delivers. 'Ambiguity' is the opposite, 'submission' relates to yielding, and 'principle' refers to a moral code rather than a state of belief.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': Who does 'she' refer to?

key_points: 'She' refers to Gretl, the wife of Solomon Margolin.

sub_questions.solution: 'She' refers to Gretl, Solomon Margolin's wife, who is being quietly observed by her husband as he reflects on her suffering and compulsive housework habits.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': Why does the narrator say 'Gretl suffered in silence'?

key_points: Gretl endured pain on behalf of her two brothers
One of her brothers, Hans, was a Nazi — a source of deep shame she bore without complaint

sub_questions.solution: The narrator says Gretl suffered in silence because she bore pain caused by her two brothers without expressing it openly. Most significantly, one of her brothers — Hans — was a Nazi, which would have been a source of profound shame, moral anguish, and social stigma. Rather than speaking of this burden, she repressed it, channelling her pain inward and manifesting it through compulsive domestic behaviour.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': Why was Gretl's face flushed and covered with beads of sweat?

key_points: She was going through a prolonged change of life (menopause)
She also insisted on doing all the housework herself, which was physically demanding

sub_questions.solution: Gretl's face was flushed and covered with beads of sweat due to two reasons. She was going through a prolonged change of life — a reference to menopause, which commonly causes hot flushes and perspiration. Additionally, she insisted on doing all the housework herself, including laundry, scouring the oven, and polishing windows, despite the family being able to afford a maid, making physical exertion a constant factor.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': What do you infer from the statement, 'He earned more than enough to pay for a maid, yet Gretl insisted on doing all the housework herself'?

key_points: Gretl's insistence on all housework despite financial means suggests a psychological compulsion
The housework serves as a coping mechanism or obsessive need for control

sub_questions.solution: This statement reveals that Gretl's obsessive housework is not driven by necessity but by a psychological compulsion. Despite her husband's comfortable income, she refuses help, suggesting that the activity satisfies a deep internal need — possibly for control, routine, or emotional distraction from unspoken suffering. Her behaviour has become a 'mania', as the narrator explicitly states, indicating that the housework is her way of managing grief, repressed trauma, and inner turmoil.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': How does she demonstrate her manic behaviour?

key_points: She does all the housework herself including laundry
She scours the oven every day
She polishes the sixteenth-floor windows without a safety belt

sub_questions.solution: Gretl demonstrates her manic behaviour through extreme, relentless dedication to housework. She refuses to hire a maid and personally handles all domestic tasks including laundry. She scours the oven every single day and, most dangerously, polishes the windows of their apartment on the sixteenth floor without wearing a safety belt — a reckless act that underscores the degree to which her compulsion has overridden rational self-preservation.

sub_questions.text_english: Part I, Extract (b) — 'A Wedding in Brownsville': Which word is the apt synonym for 'mania'?
sub_questions.solution: Option D, 'obsession', is the apt synonym for 'mania' in this context. Mania here refers to an overwhelming, uncontrollable compulsion to perform housework, which is precisely what an obsession means. Apathy means indifference, depression refers to low mood, and tranquility means calmness — all opposite to mania.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': What does the phrase 'his honour'd Bones' indicate about the poet's attitude towards Shakespeare?

key_points: Deep reverence and admiration for Shakespeare
Shakespeare is treated as a figure deserving honour even in death

sub_questions.solution: The phrase 'his honour'd Bones' indicates that the poet Milton holds Shakespeare in the highest reverence. By describing even Shakespeare's physical remains as honoured, Milton conveys that Shakespeare's greatness transcends death. The phrase reflects a tone of profound admiration and veneration, treating the playwright not merely as a talented writer but as a figure of almost sacred significance.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': Why does the poet question the need to bury Shakespeare's hallowed reliques?

key_points: Shakespeare's immortality lies in his works, not in physical monuments
Physical burial and tombs are unnecessary because his true memorial is the wonder he inspires

sub_questions.solution: Milton questions the need to bury Shakespeare's hallowed relics under a pyramid or monument because he argues that Shakespeare has already built himself a far greater memorial through his writing. Physical tombs and elaborate structures are weak witnesses of his name compared to the astonishment and wonder his works continue to inspire in every reader. Shakespeare's true immortality is intellectual and emotional, not architectural.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': What is a Star-ypointing Pyramid?

key_points: A Star-ypointing Pyramid is a tall pyramid pointing upward towards the stars — a grand physical monument built to honour the dead.

sub_questions.solution: A Star-ypointing Pyramid is a towering pyramid that points upward towards the stars — a reference to grand funerary monuments of the ancient world. Milton uses it as a symbol of physical memorials built to preserve the memory of great men after death, arguing that Shakespeare needs no such structure since his works are a living monument.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': What does the poet call as 'weak witness of thy name'?

key_points: Physical monuments — piled stones, pyramids, and grand tombs
They are inadequate compared to the living monument of Shakespeare's literary legacy

sub_questions.solution: The poet calls physical monuments — the labour of piling stones, constructing pyramids, and grand funerary structures — 'weak witness of thy name'. Milton argues that such material tributes are insufficient and feeble compared to the immortality Shakespeare has earned through his works. The real testament to his greatness is the wonder he has inspired across generations of readers, not any stone or structure.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': How has Shakespeare built himself a 'live-long Monument'?

key_points: Through his plays and poetry that fill readers with wonder and astonishment
His works live in the hearts and minds of readers across generations

sub_questions.solution: Shakespeare has built himself a live-long monument not through stone or pyramid but through his extraordinary writing. Milton states that Shakespeare has built this eternal monument in the wonder and astonishment of his readers — every reader amazed and moved by his works becomes part of that living monument. Unlike physical structures that crumble, this monument of words, emotion, and human truth grows stronger with each passing generation.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (a) — 'On Shakespear. 1630': Which word is an apt antonym of 'astonishing'?
sub_questions.solution: Option C, 'unremarkable', is the apt antonym of 'astonishing'. Astonishing means causing great surprise or wonder, while unremarkable means ordinary and not worthy of attention. Options A and D are synonyms of astonishing, and 'invisible' relates to visibility rather than impressiveness.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': Why, according to the poet, has pity become a necessity?

key_points: Pity exists only because humans have created poverty
Without the poor, there would be no one to pity — society manufactures suffering to justify the virtue of compassion

sub_questions.solution: According to Blake, pity has become a necessity because human society has manufactured the conditions that require it. He argues that pity would not exist if people had not created poverty — the existence of the poor gives the privileged an opportunity to feel and display pity. Thus, pity is not a naturally occurring virtue but a social construct that depends on inequality and suffering, making it a deeply ironic emotion.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': When, according to the poet, would there be no mercy?

key_points: There would be no mercy if all people were equally happy
Mercy requires suffering and misery to have relevance

sub_questions.solution: According to Blake, there would be no mercy if all people were as happy as the privileged. Mercy, like pity, is predicated on the existence of suffering. In a world of universal happiness and equality, there would be no one in need of mercy and therefore no opportunity to practise it. Blake is critiquing how virtues like mercy are sustained by the very inequalities they appear to oppose.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': How long can peace exist?

key_points: Peace can exist only as long as mutual fear keeps people in check
Once selfish loves grow and increase, cruelty emerges and peace is destroyed

sub_questions.solution: According to Blake, peace can exist only until mutual fear gives way to the growth of selfish desires. In the poem, peace is not a genuine state of harmony but a fragile equilibrium maintained by shared apprehension. Once self-interest and selfishness increase, cruelty — personified as a cunning hunter — sets its snare and baits, and peace is inevitably undone.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': What is meant by 'Cruelty knits a snare, And spreads his baits'?

key_points: Cruelty is personified as a cunning predator who sets traps and lures
It operates deceptively, hiding behind false virtues to ensnare people

sub_questions.solution: The phrase means that cruelty operates like a cunning hunter who carefully sets traps and places bait to catch its victims. Blake personifies cruelty as a calculating, deceptive force that does not act openly but works through disguise — hiding behind appearances of holiness and humility. The imagery suggests that cruelty is not straightforward but subtle and predatory, ensnaring people through false virtue.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': 'Only fears and tears can humble man.' Do you agree?

key_points: Blake argues humility grows from fear and weeping — not genuine spiritual virtue
A student may agree or disagree, engaging critically with Blake's cynical view

sub_questions.solution: Blake's poem suggests that humility takes root beneath the feet of cruelty, nourished by fear and tears — implying that apparent spiritual humility is actually a product of oppression and suffering. In this sense, the poem agrees that only fears and tears humble man, but views this as a disturbing truth rather than a positive one. One may partially agree that suffering produces humility, yet disagree that genuine humility cannot arise from wisdom, compassion, or moral growth independent of cruelty.

sub_questions.text_english: Part II, Extract (b) — 'The Human Abstract': Which word is the apt antonym of 'bait'?
sub_questions.solution: Option C, 'deterrent', is the apt antonym of 'bait'. Bait is something that attracts or lures, while a deterrent is something that discourages or repels. Options A and B are synonyms of bait, and 'ostentatious' means showy or pretentious, which is unrelated.

Growing shadows represent the decline of honesty and the intrusion of doubt and disguise

sub_questions.solution: In 'A Lecture Upon the Shadow', the metaphor of shadow represents the deceptions and pretences that accompany love. sub_questions.text_english: How does Tagore address the issue of women's empowerment in 'Chandalika'?

Ananda's act of asking water from her becomes a transformative moment of self-recognition and empowerment

This act awakens in her a consciousness of her own dignity and humanity, challenging both the caste system and the social subordination of women in a single transformative moment.

They symbolize her planned escape from her difficult domestic life but also the weight of the family ties she struggles to break.

questions.topic: Bergman's Approach to Film-making / The Wild Swans at Coole

sub_questions.text_english: What is Bergman's approach to film-making and how does he connect with his audience?

key_points: Bergman sees film as a deeply personal creative medium
He draws on dreams, memory, and subconscious imagery
He explores existential and spiritual themes — isolation, death, faith
He connects with audiences through emotional and psychological truth
His films demand active engagement and reflection from viewers

sub_questions.solution:
Ingmar Bergman approaches film-making as an intensely personal, almost confessional art form. He treats cinema as a medium capable of capturing dreams, memories, and the deepest movements of the human psyche. His films are not driven by conventional plot but by mood, symbol, and the exploration of existential questions — the silence of God, the fear of death, the alienation of modern life, and the complexity of human relationships.

Bergman connects with his audience not through spectacle or entertainment but through emotional and psychological honesty. He forces viewers to confront their own fears and desires by presenting characters who are deeply flawed, searching, and real. His use of close-ups, silences, and metaphorical imagery creates an intimacy that feels private rather than performative. Audiences do not merely watch Bergman's films — they experience them, carrying the emotional weight long after the final frame.

sub_questions.text_english: What is the contrast between the vitality of the swans and the decline of human life?

key_points: The swans remain unchanged — still beautiful, energetic, and paired
The poet has aged significantly since he first counted them nineteen years ago
The swans symbolise eternal vitality, passion, and constancy
The poet represents human mortality and the loss of love
Nature's indifference to human suffering is highlighted

sub_questions.solution:
In W. B. Yeats's poem 'The Wild Swans at Coole', the contrast between the swans' vitality and the poet's human decline is the emotional core of the work. The fifty-nine swans wheel and rise in great broken rings, brilliant, powerful, and seemingly ageless. Their hearts have not grown cold; they are still lovers, 'lover by lover', moving through the water with passion and constancy.

In sharp contrast, the poet stands at the water's edge as a man who has aged considerably since he first counted the swans nineteen autumns ago. He is aware of his own mortality, his waning emotional energy, and the loves he may have lost. The swans seem untouched by time, while the poet is defined by it. Their immortal vitality serves as a painful mirror to the transience of human life, love, and youth — a beauty the poet can observe but never recapture.

The quills cause painful festering wounds that can be life-threatening

Neighbours associated the house with its unusual source of funding, giving it that memorable nickname

The tooth powder venture brought him considerable wealth, and when this money was channelled into constructing his new home, neighbours associated the house with its unusual source of funding, giving it that memorable nickname.

sub_questions.text_english: What was the jungle superstition about how the tiger came to have the stripes and whom did he blame for it? Why did the tiger feel helpless in tackling the situation?

key_points: The jungle superstition held that the tiger's stripes were scorch marks from fire
The tiger blamed a mischievous monkey for tricking him near fire
The stripes were permanent — he could not remove them
The situation involved forces beyond his physical strength
It reflects the tiger's vulnerability despite his power

sub_questions.solution:
In R. K. Narayan's 'A Tiger for Malgudi', the jungle superstition holds that the tiger's stripes are actually scorch marks — burns inflicted by a mischievous creature, believed to be a monkey, who tricked the tiger into lying near fire. The tiger, proud and powerful, was humiliated by this deception and the stripes became a permanent reminder of that moment of vulnerability.

The tiger blamed the monkey for this treachery, yet felt completely helpless in addressing the situation because the damage was irreversible. No amount of strength or ferocity could remove the stripes or undo the past. This helplessness reveals an important truth about the tiger's character — despite being the most feared animal in the jungle, he is not immune to humiliation, deception, or the permanent consequences of a moment of weakness. The stripes thus symbolise both his shame and his inability to escape it.

sub_questions.text_english: Discuss the 'House of Enlightenment' and what it symbolizes for Balu.

key_points: The House of Enlightenment is the institution Balu enters in The Financial Expert
It represents a place of moral and intellectual transformation
For Balu it symbolises hope for redemption after a life of excess
It contrasts with the materialistic world his father Margayya inhabited
It signifies a spiritual and psychological turning point for Balu

sub_questions.solution:
In R. K. Narayan's 'The Financial Expert', the House of Enlightenment is a reformatory institution where Balu, Margayya's wayward son, is sent after his destructive behaviour. For Balu, who has lived a life of indulgence, irresponsibility, and moral degeneration, the House of Enlightenment represents a profound turning point.

Symbolically, it stands in stark contrast to the world of his father Margayya — a world built entirely on money, manipulation, and material ambition. While Margayya spent his life chasing financial success at the cost of ethics and family, the House of Enlightenment offers Balu the possibility of inner transformation, discipline, and genuine growth.

For Balu, it symbolises hope — the possibility that even a life derailed by excess can be redirected. Narayan uses this institution to suggest that true wealth lies not in money but in moral clarity and self-knowledge, making it the thematic counterpoint to Margayya's tragic story.
